taxonomyNote: NatureServe lists this as Sonora occipitalis (Mohave Shovel-nosed Snake) following Cox et al. (2018), who proposed merging Chionactis into Sonora; Wood et al. (2014) split C. annulata from C. occipitalis, and the USFWS assessment treats the Tucson form as a subspecies.
fieldMarks: Small snake with a shovel-shaped snout and an inset lower jaw; smooth scales in 15 rows and a divided anal plate (USFWS description of the Tucson subspecies).

Coral-snake-like banding: pale yellow to cream body with 21 or more black or brown saddle-like bands across the back, with orange-red saddles between (USFWS description of the Tucson subspecies; bands vary among forms).
behavior: Burrows or 'swims' through fine sand; nocturnal and rarely seen on the surface by day, when it may lie coiled under a bush.
Active most of the year in the south and in the warmer months in the north; inactive in cold and extreme heat.
Eats insects, spiders, scorpions and centipedes; lays eggs underground in spring.
habitat: Sparsely vegetated desert with fine, wind-blown sand: sandy flats, washes, dunes and scrub bases; less often rocky slopes.
Uses sand and other animals' burrows for cover.
range: Mojave, Sonoran and Colorado deserts of southern California, southern Nevada, northwestern Arizona, Baja California and northwestern Sonora, below about 1,400 m in California.
